title: Indian Money for Grade 1: Teach Rupees, Coins & Notes to Kids + Free Quiz
meta_title: Indian Money for Grade 1 (Rupees & Coins) + Quiz
meta_desc: Teach Indian money for Grade 1: recognise rupee coins and notes, count small amounts and make simple totals, with a free quiz and printable worksheet.
excerpt: A six-year-old at the kirana shop counter learns money faster than at any desk. Here is how I teach Indian money for Grade 1, coins first, then simple counting, with a quick quiz to check what stuck.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a six-year-old a ₹10 note and a ₹5 coin and ask which buys more, and plenty will point at the coin — it is heavier, shinier, it feels like more. That single confusion is the heart of teaching Indian money for Grade 1: a child has to learn that value is a label we agree on, not something you can feel in your palm. The good news is that this is one topic where the best classroom is a real kirana shop, not a worksheet, and most Grade 1 children pick it up faster than their parents expect.

In my experience teaching six-year-olds, money clicks when you keep it small and physical. Real coins on the table. Small whole-rupee amounts, nothing above ₹100. No paise, no change-making with decimals — that is a Grade 3 or 4 job. For now the goal is simpler and more useful: recognise our coins and notes, know that a bigger coin is not always worth more, and count a small handful up to a total.

Start with the coins and notes we actually use

Before any counting, a child needs to recognise the money itself. In everyday Indian use that means four coins — ₹1, ₹2, ₹5 and ₹10 — and the smaller notes: ₹10, ₹20, ₹50 and ₹100. Notice that ₹10 comes as both a coin and a note; showing a child both, side by side, is a lovely early lesson that the same value can wear two different costumes.

MoneyTypeWhat it buys (roughly)
₹1CoinA single toffee
₹2CoinA small candy
₹5CoinOne chocolate
₹10Coin or noteA packet of biscuits
₹20NoteA short auto ride
₹50NoteA colouring book
₹100NoteA small toy

Do not rush to name all seven in one sitting. I usually introduce the four coins first over a few days, because coins are what a child handles at the shop counter, and add the notes once the coins are secure.

The big lesson: size does not equal value

Here is the counter-intuitive bit every Grade 1 child trips over. The ₹1 and ₹2 coins are often larger than the ₹5 coin, yet worth less. A ₹10 note is thin and floppy, yet worth more than the chunky ₹5 coin in the same hand. Children reason from size because, for a five-year-old, bigger has always meant more — a bigger biscuit, a bigger balloon.

The fix is not a lecture. It is a game. Put a ₹5 coin and a ₹2 coin on the table and ask, ‘Which one would you rather have to buy a chocolate?’ When they pick wrong, do not correct them — take them to buy the chocolate and let the shopkeeper settle it. Reality is a firmer teacher than any parent.

Counting a small handful of coins

Once a child recognises each coin, counting a mixed handful is the next step. The trick that works is counting on, not restarting from one for each coin. Lay the coins out and count up: a ₹5, then a ₹2, then a ₹1 becomes ‘five… six, seven… eight.’

  • Sort first: put same-value coins together before counting.
  • Start from the biggest coin and count down to the smallest — it keeps the running total simple.
  • Say the total out loud and touch each coin as you go.
  • Keep the total under ₹100 and stick to whole rupees.

A word of honest caution: mixing many different coins at once overwhelms a Grade 1 child. Begin with two coins, then three. I would not push past four or five coins in a single count until well into the year.

Making an amount in more than one way

The idea that surprises children most is that the same amount can be built in different ways. ₹5 can be one ₹5 coin, or five ₹1 coins, or a ₹2 plus a ₹2 plus a ₹1. Ask ‘how else can we make ₹5?’ and let them hunt for combinations with real coins. This quietly builds addition and flexible thinking at the same time, and it is the exact skill they will use at a real till when the shopkeeper is out of change.

Pretend-play beats flashcards

Set up a shop on the dining table. Price a few items — a ₹5 chocolate, a ₹10 packet of biscuits, a ₹2 toffee. Give your child a small purse of coins and let them pay, take change, and be the shopkeeper by turns. Ten minutes of pretend shopping teaches more about Indian money for Grade 1 than a page of matching exercises, because the child has a reason to count carefully: they want the chocolate.

A gentle weekly routine

Little and often wins. Two short sessions of recognising coins, one session counting a small handful, and one pretend-shop game a week is plenty. Fold it into real life — let them hand over the coins for the auto, or count the change from the vegetable seller. Money is the one part of the Grade 1 syllabus that is genuinely everywhere, so use that.

One caveat worth repeating: resist the urge to introduce paise, rupee-and-paise notation, or subtraction for change. Keep it to whole rupees up to about ₹100 this year. Get recognition and simple counting rock-solid now, and the harder change-making in later grades becomes almost easy.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The short quiz below checks exactly what matters at this stage — naming a coin or note, counting a small set, spotting which coins make an amount, and judging which is worth more. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has plenty of coin-counting and shop questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 1 Indian Money Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on rupee coins and notes, counting a small handful, and making amounts. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 1 Indian money: coins, notes and simple counting

questions.q: Which of these is a coin, not a note?
You have one ₹5 coin and one ₹2 coin. How much is that?
questions.explanation: Count on from the bigger coin: five, then two more makes seven. ₹5 + ₹2 = ₹7.
Five ₹1 coins add up to ₹5. Two ₹2 coins make only ₹4.
A ₹5 coin is worth more than a ₹2 coin, even though the ₹2 coin can look bigger. Size does not decide value.

questions.q: A chocolate costs ₹10. You have one ₹5 coin and two ₹2 coins. How much more do you need?

questions.explanation: Count in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. That is five ₹2 coins.

questions.q: Which note would you use to pay a ₹20 auto fare exactly?
questions.explanation: A single ₹20 note pays the ₹20 fare exactly, with no change needed.

questions.q: You have a ₹10 note and a ₹5 coin. How much money is that?
questions.explanation: ₹10 + ₹5 = ₹15. The note and the coin add together.

faq.q: When should a Grade 1 child learn Indian money?
faq.a: Most children meet coins and notes during Grade 1, around age 6. Aim for recognising the ₹1, ₹2, ₹5 and ₹10 coins and the smaller notes, and counting a small handful — not change-making with paise, which comes later.

faq.q: Why does my child think a bigger coin is worth more?
faq.a: Because for a five-year-old, bigger has always meant more. The ₹1 and ₹2 coins are often larger than the ₹5 coin, so the fix is a real shop trip where value, not size, decides what a chocolate costs.

faq.q: Should I use real coins or printed pictures?
faq.a: Real coins, every time. A child needs to feel and sort actual money to learn it. Save printed pictures and worksheets for practice once they already recognise the real thing.

faq.q: Do we need to teach paise in Grade 1?
faq.a: No. Keep it to whole rupees up to about ₹100 this year. Recognising coins and notes and counting small amounts is plenty — paise and rupee-paise notation belong in later grades.
